title: The Entire Story of Ancient Rome
about: A calm retelling of the history of ancient Rome, from the first huts on the Palatine to the end of the Western Empire. The founding story of Romulus and Remus is told as a legend.
sources: Mary Beard, SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome (2015)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita (Book 1, for the legends)

chapters.title: The Seven Hills by the River
chapters.text:
Welcome. Tonight we are going to walk, very slowly, through the whole long story of ancient Rome. There is nothing you need to remember, and nothing you need to follow closely. If you drift away halfway through a sentence, that is perfectly fine. The story will keep going quietly without you.

Take a slow breath in, and let it out again. And one more, a little slower this time.

Let us begin in a green valley in the middle of Italy, almost three thousand years ago. A wide river winds through it, brown and unhurried. Its name is the Tiber. On either side of the river the land rises into low, rounded hills, covered with grass and oak trees, and in the evening the mist gathers in the hollows between them.

There are seven of these hills, and the Romans would later know each of them by name. The Palatine. The Capitoline. The Aventine. The Quirinal, the Viminal, the Esquiline and the Caelian. For now they are only quiet places where shepherds keep their sheep, where small huts with straw roofs stand in little clusters, and where smoke from cooking fires drifts up into the evening air.

The people who lived here spoke an early form of Latin. They kept cattle and pigs, grew barley and beans, and carried water up from the river in clay jars. Archaeologists have found the outlines of their huts on the Palatine Hill, small oval shapes pressed into the rock where wooden posts once stood.

Much later, the Romans told a legend about how their city began. It is a legend, not history, but they loved it, and they told it to their children for many centuries. In the story, twin brothers named Romulus and Remus were left beside the river as babies. A she-wolf found them and cared for them, and later a kind shepherd raised them as his own sons.

When the twins grew up, the legend says, they decided to build a city on the hills where they had been found. They could not agree on which hill to choose, and in the end Romulus built his walls on the Palatine. The city took his name, and so it was called Rome. The Romans even gave the founding a date, the year we now call seven hundred and fifty-three before Christ.

Historians today think that Rome grew more slowly than that, as small villages on the hills joined together over many generations. The low ground between the hills was marshy, and over time people drained it and laid down gravel and stone. That drained valley became a meeting place, and later the great Forum, the heart of the city.

But all of that is still far in the future. For now, there is only the river, moving quietly in the dark, the soft outlines of the hills, a few lights in the doorways of the huts, and the sound of sheep settling down for the night.

chapters.title: The Kings of Rome
chapters.text:
In the earliest days, Rome was ruled by kings. The Romans later remembered seven of them, one after another, although historians are not sure how much of those old stories is true. Some of the kings may have been real people, and some may have grown larger in memory with every telling.

The second king, the stories say, was a calm and thoughtful man called Numa. He was remembered not for battles but for ceremonies and for the calendar. It was said that he arranged the months of the year and set out the days for festivals, so that the farmers knew when to sow and when to give thanks.

To the north of Rome lived a people called the Etruscans. They built towns on hilltops, made fine pottery and bronze, and painted the walls of their tombs with scenes of music, feasting and dancing. Some of the later kings of Rome were Etruscan, and they brought many of their skills with them.

Under these kings, Rome slowly changed. The marshy valley was drained by a great covered channel, the Cloaca Maxima, which carried the water down into the Tiber. Parts of it are still there today, deep under the streets, and water still flows through it in the dark.

On the Capitoline Hill a large temple was begun, dedicated to Jupiter, the chief god of the Romans. Its roof was decorated with figures of painted clay, and from its steps you could look out over the whole small city, the river, and the fields beyond.

Life in those days moved with the seasons. In spring the fields were ploughed with oxen. In summer the barley turned gold and was cut by hand. In autumn the grapes were gathered and pressed, and in winter families stayed close to the fire, mending tools and telling stories.

The kings did not last forever. The seventh and last of them, remembered as Tarquin the Proud, was not loved by the people. In the year five hundred and nine before Christ, according to Roman tradition, the leading families of the city sent him away and decided that Rome would never again have a king.

It is a remarkable decision, when you think about it slowly. For hundreds of years afterwards, the word king was almost a forbidden word in Rome. The Romans would accept powerful generals, strict officials and grand ceremonies, but the title of king they refused, again and again.

And so, on a quiet morning long ago, the city on the seven hills began something new. The temple on the Capitoline stood finished in the sunlight, the river kept flowing as it always had, and the people of Rome began to govern themselves in a different way.

chapters.title: The Republic
chapters.text:
The new form of government was called the Republic, from the Latin words res publica, which mean the public thing, or the affairs of the people. Instead of a king, Rome would be led by officials who were chosen for a limited time.

At the top were two consuls. They were elected every year, and there were always two of them, so that neither could become too powerful alone. When their year was over, they stepped down, and two new consuls took their place.

Beside the consuls stood the Senate, a council of older and experienced men from the leading families. The Senate met in a building near the Forum, and its members sat on long benches, wrapped in white woollen togas with a broad purple stripe along the edge.

The Romans liked to write four letters on their buildings, their coins and their standards: S P Q R. They stand for Senatus Populusque Romanus, the Senate and the People of Rome. You can still see those letters today, carved into old stone, and even on the covers of drains in the modern city.

Not everyone in Rome had the same rights. There were the old wealthy families, called patricians, and the ordinary citizens, called plebeians. For a long time the two groups argued about power and fairness, and slowly, step by step, the plebeians gained more say in how the city was run.

One important step came around the year four hundred and fifty before Christ. The laws of Rome were written down for the first time on twelve tablets and set up in the Forum, so that everyone could read them. Roman children learned these Twelve Tables by heart for generations afterwards.

Imagine the Forum on a quiet morning in those years. The paving stones are still cool from the night. A few shopkeepers are opening their wooden shutters. Two senators walk slowly past the temples, talking in low voices. Somewhere a dog is asleep in a patch of early sunlight.

Over the next centuries, Rome grew. It made alliances with neighbouring towns, and sometimes it fought with them. Slowly the city on the seven hills became the leading power in central Italy, and then in the whole Italian peninsula.

The Romans were proud of their Republic. They believed that a good citizen should be modest, hard-working and loyal to the city. They told stories of a farmer named Cincinnatus, who was called from his plough to lead Rome in a time of danger, and who, once the danger had passed, simply went home and returned to his fields.

That story, too, may have grown a little in the telling. But it shows what the Romans hoped to be. And so the Republic went on, year after year, with its two consuls, its Senate on their long benches, and its laws on twelve tablets in the morning light.

chapters.title: Roads, Water and Stone
chapters.text:
The Romans were patient builders. Wherever their influence spread, they built roads, bridges, aqueducts and towns, and many of those works lasted far longer than anyone at the time could have imagined.

The most famous of the early roads was the Via Appia, the Appian Way. Work on it began in the year three hundred and twelve before Christ, and it ran south from Rome, mile after mile, in long straight lines across the countryside.

A Roman road was built in layers. First the workers dug a trench. Then they filled it with larger stones, then smaller stones and gravel, and finally they laid flat paving stones on top, fitted together closely. The surface was slightly curved, so that rainwater would run off to the sides.

Along the roads stood milestones, tall stone markers that told travellers how far they had come. Every so often there were places to rest, to water the horses and to sleep for the night. Some stretches of the Appian Way can still be walked today, under tall umbrella pines, with the old paving stones worn smooth by more than two thousand years of footsteps.

The Romans also brought water to their city from far away. They built aqueducts, long channels that carried fresh water from springs in the hills. Most of each aqueduct ran underground or along the ground, sloping down so gently that you would hardly notice it. Only where a valley had to be crossed did they raise the water up on those famous rows of arches.

The first aqueduct of Rome, the Aqua Appia, was built in the same year as the Appian Way. Over the following centuries many more were added, until the city had fountains on almost every street corner, and the sound of running water could be heard day and night.

The Romans also learned to make a kind of concrete. They mixed lime with a volcanic ash found near the Bay of Naples, and they discovered that this mixture became very strong and could even harden under water. With it they built harbours, domes and vaults that still stand today.

The most beautiful example is the Pantheon in Rome, built in the time of the emperor Hadrian. Its great round dome is made of concrete, and at the very top there is an open circle, called the oculus, through which the sky can be seen. On sunny days a round patch of light moves slowly across the floor and the walls, like the hand of a very large and very quiet clock.

When it rains, the rain falls gently through that opening and drains away through small holes in the floor. You can imagine standing there in the evening, in the cool, dim space under the dome, listening to the soft sound of drops falling from the sky into the middle of the room.

chapters.title: Carthage and the Middle Sea
chapters.text:
As Rome grew, it began to look beyond Italy, out across the sea. The Romans called the Mediterranean simply Mare Nostrum, our sea, although for a long time it was not theirs at all.

On the coast of North Africa, in what is now Tunisia, stood the great city of Carthage. It had been founded long before by Phoenician sailors and traders, and it had a magnificent round harbour, with room for many ships, and a busy market full of goods from every shore.

Rome and Carthage became rivals. Over more than a hundred years, between the years two hundred and sixty-four and one hundred and forty-six before Christ, they fought three long wars, which the Romans called the Punic Wars. We will not linger on the battles tonight. It is enough to say that they were long, that both sides suffered, and that many years passed in between them.

There is one part of the story that people have told for centuries. A general of Carthage named Hannibal decided to reach Italy not by sea, but over land. In the year two hundred and eighteen before Christ, he led his army from Spain, across rivers and through southern France, and then over the high, snowy passes of the Alps.

With him came elephants. Nobody knows exactly how many survived the crossing, and historians still debate which mountain pass he used. But you can picture the long line of soldiers and animals winding slowly up the mountain paths, the snow on the peaks, the cold blue air, and the great grey elephants stepping carefully over the stones.

Hannibal stayed in Italy for many years, but in the end he could not take Rome. The Romans were stubborn and patient. They rebuilt their armies, they built new fleets, and finally the war moved to Africa, where Hannibal was defeated.

In the third war, in the year one hundred and forty-six before Christ, Carthage itself was taken and destroyed. In the same year the Romans also took the old Greek city of Corinth. From then on, Rome was the strongest power around the whole Middle Sea.

Rome also learned a great deal from the Greeks. Roman families had Greek teachers for their children. Greek statues were copied and placed in Roman gardens. Greek plays were translated into Latin, and Greek ideas about philosophy, medicine and mathematics travelled into Roman homes.

Now, picture a merchant ship in those calmer years, sailing slowly across the sea on a summer evening. Its sail is full of warm wind, its hold is full of jars of olive oil and wine, and on deck a sailor sits with his back against the mast, watching the coastline turn violet in the fading light.

chapters.title: Caesar and the End of the Republic
chapters.text:
By the last century before Christ, Rome had become very large and very rich. But the Republic, which had been made for a small city, struggled to govern so many lands. Powerful generals with loyal armies began to compete for influence, and the old balance began to wobble.

The most famous of these generals was Gaius Julius Caesar. He was clever, ambitious and an excellent writer. For about eight years he led Roman armies in Gaul, the land that is now France and Belgium, and he wrote his own calm, clear account of those years, which students of Latin still read today.

In the year forty-nine before Christ, the Senate ordered Caesar to give up his army. Instead, he led his soldiers across a small river in northern Italy called the Rubicon, which marked the border of his province. Crossing it with an army meant there was no turning back. Even today, people say crossing the Rubicon when they mean taking a step that cannot be undone.

A civil war followed, and Caesar won it. He returned to Rome and was named dictator, at first for a limited time, and later for life. He made many changes. One of the most lasting was a new calendar, with three hundred and sixty-five days and an extra day every fourth year. It is called the Julian calendar, and the calendar we use today grew out of it.

The month of July still carries his name. Every summer, when people write the date, they are quietly remembering Julius Caesar without even thinking about it.

But many senators feared that Caesar wanted to become a king, and in Rome that was the one thing they could not accept. On the Ides of March, the fifteenth day of March, in the year forty-four before Christ, a group of senators killed him at a meeting of the Senate. We will leave that moment there, without lingering on it.

His death did not save the Republic. Instead, more years of conflict followed. Caesar had named his great-nephew, a young man called Octavian, as his heir. Octavian was quiet and careful, and he was patient in a way that his rivals were not.

Step by step, Octavian gathered support, and in the end he defeated his last great rival, Mark Antony, and the queen of Egypt, Cleopatra. After many long years of war, there was finally only one man left at the centre of Roman power.

Imagine the evening after the last of those wars. The ships return slowly to their harbours. Soldiers walk home along the long straight roads. In farmhouses across Italy, families light their lamps and sit down to supper, hoping that the years ahead will be quieter than the years behind.

chapters.title: Augustus and the Long Peace
chapters.text:
In the year twenty-seven before Christ, the Senate gave Octavian a new name: Augustus, which means something like the honoured one, or the revered one. Historians usually call him the first Roman emperor, although he himself was careful never to call himself king.

Augustus kept the old offices of the Republic. There were still consuls and there was still a Senate. But in practice, the real power now rested with him, and with the emperors who came after him.

What followed was a long period of relative peace inside the empire. The Romans called it the Pax Romana, the Roman peace. It lasted, more or less, for about two hundred years. There were still wars at the borders, and life was not peaceful for everyone, but many regions knew calmer times than they had known for generations.

Augustus liked to say that he had found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble. New temples, theatres and public buildings rose in the city. Gardens were laid out, and old buildings were repaired and decorated.

The month of August is named after him, just as July is named after Caesar. So two of our summer months, warm and long, still carry the names of two Romans who lived more than two thousand years ago.

During these long years of peace, trade flowed along the roads and across the sea. Grain came by ship from Egypt. Olive oil came from Spain. Wine came from Gaul and Greece. Silk sometimes arrived from much farther east, passed from trader to trader along long routes until it reached Roman markets.

Across the empire, towns were built in a similar pattern. There was a forum in the centre, temples, a basilica for business and courts, public baths, and often a theatre or an arena. A traveller arriving in a Roman town in Britain or Syria would have found many familiar things.

Latin was spoken in the western half of the empire, and Greek in the eastern half. Educated people often spoke both. Letters travelled by official messengers along the roads, changing horses at stations along the way, so that news could cross great distances in a few weeks.

Augustus lived a long life and died in the year fourteen after Christ, in the month that now bears his name. He was followed by many emperors, some wise and some foolish, some calm and some cruel. But the great machine of the empire kept turning, slowly, year after year.

Picture a quiet road in the countryside during those long peaceful years. It is late afternoon. A cart pulled by two oxen creaks slowly past a milestone. A boy walks beside it with a stick, humming a song. Far away, on a low hill, the roof tiles of a farmhouse glow orange in the setting sun.

chapters.title: A Day in the City
chapters.text:
Let us spend a quiet day in the city of Rome, at the height of the empire, when perhaps around a million people lived there. Nobody counted exactly, but it was one of the largest cities in the ancient world.

The day began early. As the sky turned pale, bakers were already at work, and the smell of fresh bread drifted through the narrow streets. In the town of Pompeii, near Naples, archaeologists have found round loaves of bread, baked in the year seventy-nine and preserved under volcanic ash, still divided into neat sections like a cake.

Most ordinary people lived in apartment buildings called insulae. They were several floors high, with shops on the ground floor and small rooms above. The higher you went, the cheaper and smaller the rooms became. Many people had no kitchen of their own, and bought warm food from little street counters.

The morning was a time for business. Clients visited their patrons to greet them. Shops opened their shutters. In the Forum, lawyers spoke, merchants traded, and people gathered to hear the latest news.

In the afternoon, many Romans went to the baths. The public baths were enormous buildings with warm rooms, hot rooms and cold pools, gardens, libraries and places to exercise. For a very small fee, almost anyone could spend a few hours there. Water was heated by fires below the floors, and warm air flowed through hollow spaces under the tiles.

Imagine lying back in the warm water, under a high vaulted ceiling, with the sound of voices echoing softly around the room, steam rising slowly, and a little light coming in through high windows.

Children went to small schools, if their families could afford it. They learned to read and write, often on wax tablets with a pointed stylus. They practised their letters, smoothed the wax flat again, and started over. They played with dolls, marbles made from nuts, and little wooden toys.

In the evening, families ate their main meal. Rich families reclined on couches around a low table, while poorer families sat on stools. They ate bread, beans, lentils, cheese, olives, fruit and sometimes fish or meat, and they mixed their wine with water.

In December, the Romans celebrated a festival called Saturnalia. For a few days, ordinary rules were relaxed. People exchanged small gifts, wore colourful clothes, lit candles and played games. Some of the customs of that festival may have left gentle traces in winter celebrations that came much later.

As night fell over the city, the streets grew quiet. Lamps flickered in windows. Somewhere a fountain kept splashing softly. And across the rooftops of Rome, people settled down to sleep, just as you are settling down now.

chapters.title: Walls, Faith and a Divided Empire
chapters.text:
As the years passed, the empire grew to its greatest size. Around the year one hundred and seventeen after Christ, under the emperor Trajan, it stretched from Britain in the north-west to Egypt in the south and Mesopotamia in the east.

Such a large empire was hard to protect. The emperor Hadrian, who followed Trajan, decided that the empire should stop growing and instead guard what it already had. In the north of Britain, starting around the year one hundred and twenty-two, his soldiers built a long stone wall from coast to coast.

Hadrian's Wall still runs across the green hills of northern England today. You can walk beside it for days, past the remains of small forts and watchtowers, with sheep grazing quietly in the fields and the wind moving through the long grass.

Life on the frontier was often calm and a little dull. Soldiers wrote letters home, asked for warm socks, and invited friends to birthday parties. Some of these letters, written on thin wooden tablets, have survived at a fort called Vindolanda, so we can still read their words today.

In the third century, the empire went through difficult times. Emperors came and went quickly, and there were troubles at the borders and in the economy. Eventually, the emperor Diocletian decided that the empire was too big for one ruler, and he shared the work of governing among several emperors.

In the early fourth century, the emperor Constantine became the first emperor to support Christianity. In the year three hundred and thirty, he founded a new capital in the east, on the site of the old Greek town of Byzantium, where Europe and Asia almost touch. It was called Constantinople, and today it is the city of Istanbul.

Constantinople stood on hills above the water, with harbours on either side. Ships came and went through the narrow strait, carrying grain, spices and travellers. The new capital grew quickly into one of the largest and richest cities in the world.

After the death of the emperor Theodosius in the year three hundred and ninety-five, the empire was divided for good between his two sons. From then on there was a western half, governed mostly from Italy, and an eastern half, governed from Constantinople.

The two halves still thought of themselves as one Roman world. They shared laws, coins and traditions. But slowly, over the following decades, their paths began to separate, like two rivers that flow out of the same lake and then wander off through different valleys.

Picture the evening light on the long wall in northern Britain, the stones turning golden, a soldier pulling his cloak a little tighter, and far away, at the other end of the empire, the lamps of Constantinople beginning to shine across the dark water.

chapters.title: The Long Evening of Rome
chapters.text:
In the fifth century, the western half of the empire grew weaker. Many peoples were moving across Europe in those years, and some of them settled inside the old borders of the empire. Some came as allies, some as rivals, and some simply as families looking for land.

The city of Rome itself was no longer the capital. The western emperors often lived in Milan, or in Ravenna, a town protected by marshes on the Adriatic coast. Ravenna is still known for its shimmering mosaics, made of thousands of tiny pieces of coloured glass and gold.

In the year four hundred and seventy-six, the last emperor in the west, a boy named Romulus Augustulus, was removed from power by a general named Odoacer. There was no great battle and no dramatic ending. The boy was sent to live quietly in a villa near Naples, and Odoacer did not take the title of emperor for himself.

Historians often use that year to mark the end of the Western Roman Empire. But for the people living at the time, life simply went on. Farmers ploughed their fields. Bakers baked their bread. Bishops looked after their towns, and Latin was still spoken in the markets.

In the east, the Roman Empire continued for almost a thousand more years. The people of Constantinople still called themselves Romans. Today we usually call that empire Byzantine, after the old name of its capital. It lasted until the year fourteen hundred and fifty-three.

So, in a way, ancient Rome did not end on a single day. It faded slowly, like the light of a long summer evening, when the sun has gone down but the sky stays bright for a long time afterwards.

And much of Rome is still with us. Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian all grew out of Latin. Many English words come from Latin too. Our calendar grew out of the one that Caesar introduced, and the names of July and August still remember two Romans.

Ideas from Roman law still shape legal systems in many countries. Roman roads still lie beneath modern roads. Roman arches still carry water, or at least the memory of water, across quiet valleys. And the Pantheon still stands in Rome, with its round open eye looking up at the sky.

Now the story is almost finished. Picture the old city one last time, late at night. The Tiber flows quietly past, as it always has. The seven hills are dark shapes against the stars. The great buildings are silent, and the only sound is the soft splash of a fountain somewhere nearby.

You can let all of it go now. The kings, the senators, the roads and the ships, the long peace and the long evening. They will all still be there tomorrow, in the pages of history, waiting quietly.

You can rest now. Let your breathing slow down. Let your shoulders sink a little deeper. There is nothing more you need to do tonight.

Goodnight.
